.eth.definition: The web3 domain ending used by the Ethereum Name Service (ENS), as in yourname.eth.

2 factor authentication.definition: An extra layer of security used to make sure that people trying to gain access to an online account are who they say they are.

2fa.definition: An extra layer of security used to make sure that people trying to gain access to an online account are who they say they are.

51% attack.definition: An attack on blockchain consensus by controlling more than half of the block-producing power on the network.

address.definition: Unique public identifier for an entity on a blockchain.

addresses.definition: Unique public identifiers for entities on a blockchain.

aggregator.definition: A tool that combines multiple sources to offer the most competitive options.

airdrop.definition: A free distribution of crypto assets to users.

allo protocol.definition: Short for Capital Allocation Protocol. An open-source protocol that enables groups to efficiently and transparently allocate pooled capital.

allowance.definition: Allows an entity, usually a smart contract, the right to use a specified amount of your tokens in a transaction.

alternative layer 1.definition: Layer 1 blockchains other than Ethereum and Bitcoin.

amm.definition: (Automated Market Maker) A trade matchmaking system, based on a public algorithm.

app.definition: An application for a computer or mobile device.

app store.definition: A digital shop for downloading computer or mobile device applications.

asynchronous.definition: Communication between multiple collaborators, where participants don’t have to be present at time of messaging.

attestation.definition: A signed confirmation that something is true. On Ethereum, validators publish attestations voting that a block is valid.

autonomy.definition: The quality of governing your own actions, rather than adhering to frameworks of others.

basenames.definition: A naming service on the Base network, giving wallets human-readable names ending in .base.eth.

batch auction.definition: A trading method that collects many orders over a short period and settles them together at one fair price.

bet.definition: Risking money in exchange for greater rewards.

blob.definition: A cheap, temporary data space in Ethereum blocks, used by Layer 2s to post their transaction batches.

block.definition: A group of transactions on the blockchain.

block builder.definition: A specialized operator that assembles transactions into new blocks, which block proposers then publish to the network.

block explorer.definition: Search and exploration tool for blockchain data.

block hash.definition: The unique identifier for each block file. Each new block refers to the block hash of the previous block to form the single-file connected blockchain.

block producer.definition: A network participant chosen to create new blocks of transactions, such as a miner or validator.

block proposer.definition: The validator node chosen by the network algorithm to select the next block to be added to the blockchain.

block reward.definition: An amount of native coin given to the proposer of a new valid block.

block space.definition: The amount of space in each block for storing transactions and data.

blockchain.definition: A system in which a record of cryptocurrency transactions is maintained across many computers around the world.

blockchain apps.definition: Blockchain applications that allow you to swap cryptocurrency, use web3 social media, make charitable donations, or even learn onchain, like at Bankless Academy.

blockchain architecture.definition: The structures for how data is stored in blockchain technology.

blockchain technology.definition: A new type of network, hosted across many computers. It's adding a new layer of digital ownership to the internet.

blockchain trilemma.definition: The problem describing the need for all 3 blockchain qualities: Security, Scalability, and Decentralization.

blockspace.definition: The amount of space in each block for storing transactions and data.

borrower.definition: Willing to pay interest to lenders in order to borrow assets.

bridge.definition: Connection that allows two different blockchain networks to communicate with each other and exchange assets.

censorship-resistant.definition: No government or company has control to determine what is or is not allowed.

central bank.definition: An institution regulating money, banks, and currency in a country.

centralization.definition: The concentration of power over an entire system under a single authority/entity.

centralized.definition: Where a single authority/entity controls the entire system.

centralized exchange.definition: (CEX) A centralized platform that coordinates cryptocurrency trading for a fee, similar to a stock exchange.

centralized exchange staking.definition: Locking tokens through a Centralized Exchange to generate rewards.

centralized services.definition: Corporations or entities that control online activities, setting rules and fees, and managing data and content in ways that often prioritize their own interests over user needs.

cex.definition: (Centralized Exchange) A platform that coordinates cryptocurrency trading for a fee, similar to a stock exchange.

chain.definition: Binds blocks of data together to form a database which cannot be altered or changed.

circulating supply.definition: The number of a specific cryptocurrency's coins or tokens publicly available for the market to trade.

coin.definition: The native asset of a blockchain mostly used as a form of currency to facilitate transactions on the network.

cold wallet.definition: A type of self-custody wallet that is stored on offline hardware.

collateral.definition: A borrower's pledge of specific asset(s) to a lender, to secure repayment of a loan.

commercial bank.definition: A bank managing money for people and businesses.

composability.definition: The ability to combine existing smart contracts and apps like building blocks to create new products.

consensus.definition: Agreement, trust, and security across a decentralized computer network like blockchains.

consensus mechanism.definition: The method by which a blockchain network judges which transactions are legitimate, and which are fraudulent.

consensus mechanisms.definition: Methods by which blockchain networks judge which transactions are legitimate, and which are fraudulent.

counterparty risk.definition: The risk that another party may not fulfill its part in an agreement.

credible neutrality.definition: A mechanism that does not discriminate for or against any specific people.

crypto.definition: (Cryptocurrency) Currencies native to the internet, not an individual country. Rather than being managed by a central bank, they’re often governed by their users.

crypto wallet.definition: An app that allows you to store your cryptocurrency, and send/receive or spend it.

cryptocurrencies.definition: Currencies native to the internet, not individual countries. Rather than being managed by a central bank, they’re often governed by their users.

cryptocurrency.definition: A currency native to the internet, not an individual country. Rather than being managed by a central bank, it’s often governed by its users.

cryptocurrency mining.definition: Verifying blockchain transactions in exchange for cryptocurrency rewards, used on Proof-of-Work networks like Bitcoin.

cryptocurrency wallet.definition: An app that allows you to store your cryptocurrency, and send/receive or spend it.

cryptography.definition: Techniques for secure communication or transaction, preventing external interference.

custodial wallet.definition: With a custodial wallet, another party controls the private keys, thus controlling access to your crypto assets.

custodian.definition: A financial institution given responsibility to secure your assets.

custom record.definition: A user-defined data entry linked to an ENS domain, letting you attach extra information, like a website or social links, beyond standard addresses.

dao.definition: (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) An organizational structure that uses blockchain technology to automate voting and management.

dapp.definition: A “decentralized application” that connects to blockchains and decentralized networks.

death spiral.definition: A self-reinforcing collapse where a falling price forces actions that push the price down further, as with some algorithmic stablecoins.

decentralization.definition: The transfer of control to many individuals rather than one single authority.

decentralized.definition: No single authority or entity controls the system.

decentralized exchange.definition: (DEX) A protocol that facilitates exchange without requiring trusted intermediaries.

decentralized finance.definition: (DeFi) A set of self-custody finance tools, hosted on a blockchain.

decentralized money.definition: Money with properties agreed on by the community, rather than set by an institution.

decentralized services.definition: (dApps) Online services that use automation to reduce fees and improve user experience.

defi.definition: (Decentralized Finance) A set of self-custody finance tools, hosted on a blockchain.

delegate.definition: Giving a specific responsibility to another person, i.e. delegation of token voting power.

delegation.definition: Giving a specific responsibility to another person, i.e. delegation of token voting power.

democracy.definition: A system of government where citizens exercise power by playing a key role in decision-making.

dex.definition: (Decentralized Exchange) A protocol that facilitates exchange without requiring trusted intermediaries.

dex aggregator.definition: Protocol that combines DEX liquidity from multiple sources in one interface.

digital signature.definition: Proof, created with your private key, that you approved a message or transaction. It works like a handwritten signature, but cannot be forged.

double-spend.definition: Spending the same digital money twice. Blockchain consensus exists to prevent this without a central authority.

earn.definition: Contributing value in exchange for rewards; money verb on the skill cube.

encryption.definition: The process of converting information into private and secure code, used to prevent unauthorized access.

epoch.definition: The time taken for a specific number of blocks to be included on any particular blockchain.

equality of opportunity.definition: A fairness principle, where everyone has the same chances to succeed regardless of their background or circumstances.

erc-20.definition: A standard for fungible tokens on Ethereum. These tokens are divisible and non-unique.

erc-721.definition: A standard for non-fungible tokens on Ethereum. These tokens have a unique digital identifier, cannot be copied, or subdivided.

erc-1155.definition: A standard for deploying both fungible and non-fungible tokens on Ethereum, under one optimized contract.

etf.definition: (Exchange-Traded Fund) An investment fund traded on the stock market, holding assets like stocks, gold, or bitcoin.

eth.definition: (Ether) Ethereum’s native cryptocurrency. Used to perform transactions on the network, run a validator node, and more.

ether.definition: (ETH) Ethereum’s native cryptocurrency. Used to perform transactions on the network, run a validator node, and more.

ethereum blockchain.definition: A public ledger documenting transactions and ownership on the Ethereum network.

ethereum mainnet.definition: Ethereum’s main Layer 1 network, where transactions carry real value. It is the settlement layer for Ethereum’s Layer 2s.

ethereum virtual machine.definition: The Ethereum Virtual Machine or EVM is a piece of software that executes smart contracts and computes the state of the Ethereum network.

fiat.definition: A national currency that, rather than being backed by a commodity like gold, derives value from the public's trust in the issuer.

finality.definition: The guarantee that a confirmed blockchain transaction is permanent and cannot be reversed or changed.

finality time.definition: The time it takes to be sure that a transaction is valid and final, meaning it won't be reversed or changed.

fomo.definition: (Fear Of Missing Out) Anxiety or apprehension about not being included in something.

fork.definition: A radical change in a blockchain network that results in two branches: one following the previous protocol, and one following a new one.

fraud.definition: In blockchain economies: Unfair or fake transactions, used to change amounts of cryptocurrency held.

fraud proof.definition: Evidence that a transaction is invalid and that fraud has occurred.

front-running.definition: Seeing someone's pending transaction and paying to get your own processed first, profiting at their expense.

fungibility.definition: The property of being interchangeable: each unit has the same value and can replace any other, like one dollar bill for another.

gas fee.definition: A transaction fee paid to use a blockchain network.

gasless transactions.definition: Transactions where the gas fee is paid in the token being traded, or covered by a sponsor, instead of the network’s native coin.

gold standard.definition: A monetary system where a country's currency has a value directly linked to gold.

gwei.definition: A unit used on the Ethereum blockchain, equal to 0.000000001 ETH (one billionth), commonly used to describe gas prices.

halving.definition: A scheduled event, roughly every four years, that cuts the reward for mining new Bitcoin in half.

hardware wallet.definition: A type of self-custody wallet that stores private keys offline in a physical hardware device.

hashing function.definition: A function that turns any input into a unique fixed-size fingerprint (hash). It is easy to compute one way, but practically impossible to reverse.

hodl.definition: (Hold On for Dear Life) Crypto slang for not selling crypto no matter what the market conditions are.

hot wallet.definition: A type of self-custody wallet that is perpetually connected to the internet.

inflation.definition: A general increase in prices and fall in the purchasing power of money.

intent.definition: A signed trade request describing the outcome you want, like “swap X for at least Y”, leaving the best route to specialists.

intermediaries.definition: Entities or services connecting people, in order to facilitate exchanges of value or information.

intermediary.definition: An entity or service connecting people, in order to facilitate an exchange of value or information.

intermediary token.definition: A token that is part of the middle of a trade route, not the starting or ending token.

interoperability.definition: The ability of different apps, tokens, and blockchains to work together and share information.

invest.definition: Putting money into an asset, like a coin or token, expecting its value to grow.

l1.definition: Layer 1 refers to a base network such as Bitcoin or Ethereum.

l2.definition: A blockchain that extends Ethereum scalability while inheriting Ethereum security.

layer 1.definition: Layer 1 refers to a base network such as Bitcoin or Ethereum.

layer 2.definition: A blockchain that extends Ethereum scalability while inheriting Ethereum security.

ledger.definition: The record of all transactions that have ever occurred.

lightning network.definition: A payment network built on top of Bitcoin, using payment channels to make everyday payments instant and cheap.

liquid.definition: In blockchain economies: The ability to easily use a digital asset in trading, or use in smart contracts.

liquid staking token.definition: Tokens representing staked Ether. Holders earn a portion of staking rewards proportional to the amounts staked.

liquidation.definition: The automatic sale of a borrower’s collateral when its value falls too low to safely cover the loan.

liquidity.definition: The quantity of a token available for trading.

liquidity pool.definition: A communal vault of tokens that facilitates permissionless token swaps.

lp.definition: (Liquidity Provider) Blockchain users who loan their tokens to protocols in exchange for a share in fees.

lsts.definition: Tokens representing staked Ether. Holders earn a portion of staking rewards proportional to the amounts staked.

mainnet.definition: The main, live blockchain network where transactions carry real value, as opposed to test networks. Often refers to Ethereum’s Layer 1.

market cap.definition: The total value of a given token, or market sector.

max supply.definition: The maximum number of coins or tokens that will ever exist for a particular cryptocurrency.

memecoin.definition: A cryptocurrency token themed on an internet meme, often with no purpose or utility.

meta-aggregator.definition: A tool that brings together other aggregators into an extra overview layer.

mev.definition: (Maximal Extractable Value) Profit block producers can make by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions within blocks.

miner.definition: A participant in a Proof-of-Work network, like Bitcoin, who competes to propose new blocks in exchange for rewards.

mining.definition: The Proof-of-Work process of verifying transactions and adding new blocks to the blockchain, in exchange for rewards.

mint.definition: Issuing new fungible or non-fungible cryptocurrency tokens on a given blockchain.

monetary policy.definition: How a central bank manages the amount of money circulating in an economy.

money.definition: A medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value, used to facilitate transactions for goods and services.

multi-token standard.definition: A token standard, like ERC-1155, that supports both fungible and non-fungible tokens in one smart contract.

network governance.definition: The process by which a decentralized community reaches agreement on network features/upgrades.

neutrality.definition: The principle of treating all participants equally, without bias towards any user or group.

nft.definition: (Non-fungible Token) A token with a unique ID that cannot be replicated, as compared to a fungible token like Ether that has no unique identifier.

node.definition: A computer running blockchain software that stores a copy of the ledger and helps verify the network.

node operator.definition: A member of the Ethereum community, running a validator node to process transactions on the network.

non-custodial wallet.definition: (AKA: Self-custody wallet) With a non-custodial wallet, you have sole control of your private keys, which in turn control your crypto assets.

offchain.definition: Any action or data that happens outside the blockchain, like on regular servers or in signed messages.

onchain.definition: Recorded on a blockchain network. Refers to actions performed on cryptocurrency networks like Ethereum.

onchain governance.definition: The automated system that mediates changes to a blockchain’s structure.

onchain identity.definition: A public identity built from your blockchain activity and records, such as an ENS name linked to your wallet address.

onramp.definition: A service that converts regular money, like dollars, into cryptocurrency. Offramps do the reverse.

open internet.definition: An accessible digital space where information, services, and communication are available to all users without control by centralized entities.

open source.definition: Software with source code that anyone can inspect, modify, and enhance.

optimistic rollup.definition: A Layer 2 rollup that assumes all transactions in its batch are valid, unless proven false by a fraud proof during a challenge period.

oracle.definition: A service that brings outside information, like market prices, onto the blockchain for smart contracts to use.

order book.definition: A list of buy and sell offers at different prices. Traditional exchanges match trades from this list.

otc.definition: (Over the Counter) Trades made directly with private entities.

over the counter.definition: (OTC) Trades made directly with private entities.

password manager.definition: An app that securely stores your passwords and can generate strong, unique ones for each account.

payment channel.definition: Allows two parties to transact multiple times without the need for each transaction to be recorded on the blockchain.

peer.definition: A person or entity treated as an equal.

peer-to-peer.definition: Connections between multiple parties that don’t require an intermediary.

peg.definition: Method of maintaining value equivalence between two or more assets.

permissionless.definition: Not requiring the permission of any entity.

phishing.definition: A type of social engineering attack where the attacker poses as a trusted person or organization to trick victims into sharing sensitive information or sending them money.

poap.definition: A POAP (Proof of Attendance Protocol) is a badge that keeps a reliable record of life experiences in your wallet, like for example successfully completing a lesson.

pos.definition: (Proof of Stake) Consensus where validators lock up stake to secure the network.

price impact.definition: How much your own trade moves the price on a DEX, based on the trade’s size.

primary name.definition: The ENS name linked to your wallet address, letting apps display your name instead of a long address.

private key.definition: A private key grants access to your wallet, allowing you to send crypto assets to other wallets.

private transaction routing.definition: Sending transactions directly to block builders instead of the public queue, hiding them from front-running bots.

proof of stake.definition: A consensus method that randomly chooses block producers based on the stake each participant has locked into the protocol.

proof of work.definition: A consensus method where miners spend computing power (the “work”) competing to propose valid blocks.

proof-of-stake.definition: A blockchain consensus method that selects validator nodes based on the amount of stake locked by the node.

pseudonymous.definition: Acting under a chosen name that hides your real identity.

public.definition: Public blockchains allow anyone to view the blockchain ledger.

public good.definition: A public good is a commodity or service that is available to all members of society.

public key.definition: A code created from your private key that is safe to share. Your wallet address is derived from your public key.

quadratic funding.definition: A crowd-funding mechanism that amplifies available resources with individual donations of any size acting as votes. The broader the support, the bigger the impact!

recovery phrase.definition: A recovery phrase is a list of 12 to 24 words, used to generate your wallet's public key and private key.

restaking.definition: Reusing staked Ether tokens to help secure and validate other protocols, in exchange for rewards.

retropgf.definition: (Retroactive Public Goods Funding) A mechanism for funding projects, based on their historical impact.

rollup.definition: A Layer 2 scaling solution that processes many transactions away from the main chain, then posts them in one batch, increasing throughput and lowering costs.

sandwich attack.definition: An attack where bots place trades right before and after yours to move the price, profiting at your expense.

satoshi nakamoto.definition: The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin. To this day, nobody knows their real identity.

scalability.definition: A blockchain’s capability to handle a growing amount of work, transactions, and usage with minimal disruption for users.

scam-token.definition: A cryptocurrency token that is launched for the sole purpose of stealing investor funds.

scarce.definition: The state of being in short supply.

security.definition: Ability of a blockchain to withstand hacking attempts, code exploits, and economic exploits among other attacks, and continue to function as normal.

seed phrase.definition: Group of random words generated by a wallet on setup, they act as the master key to ALL accounts controlled by that wallet. NEVER SHARE YOUR SEED PHRASE WITH ANYONE FOR ANY REASON.

self-custodial.definition: A means of holding your assets where only you have access to them.

self-custody.definition: A means of holding your assets where only you have access to them.

self-custody wallet.definition: (AKA: Non-custodial wallet) With a self-custody wallet, you have sole control of your private keys, which in turn control your crypto assets.

settlement layer.definition: The “lowest” level of a blockchain that records the details of asset exchange from finalized transactions. Mainnet Ethereum is the settlement layer for Ethereum layer 2 scaling solutions.

settlement time.definition: The time needed for a transaction to be confirmed.

sharding.definition: The process of splitting a single blockchain into multiple chains that all run together in parallel to increase scalability.

sidechain.definition: A separate blockchain that runs in parallel to a main blockchain, connected by a bridge, with its own validators and security.

slashed.definition: A penalty where a validator loses part of its stake for provably cheating on a Proof-of-Stake blockchain.

slashing.definition: A penalty on Proof-of-Stake networks that destroys part of a validator’s stake for provable cheating, like signing two conflicting blocks.

slippage.definition: The difference between the price you expect and the price you get when your trade executes.

slippage tolerance.definition: The maximum price change you accept for a trade. If the price moves more than this, the trade is cancelled.

smart account.definition: A wallet account powered by a smart contract; another name for a smart wallet.

smart contract.definition: Computerized code that executes terms of a contract automatically.

smart wallet.definition: A wallet powered by a smart contract instead of a single private key, enabling features like account recovery and passkey logins.

social engineering.definition: Manipulating someone into sharing sensitive or confidential information such as passwords or seed phrases.

solo staker.definition: A node operator running an independent validator node.

solo staking.definition: Running your own validator node to process transactions in Proof-of-Stake systems.

solver.definition: A specialist that competes with others to execute a user’s intent at the best possible price.

spend.definition: Using your crypto assets to pay for goods or services.

spot etf.definition: An ETF that holds the actual asset, like bitcoin, letting people invest in it through the traditional stock market.

stablecoin.definition: A token designed to hold a steady value, usually pegged 1:1 to a currency like the US dollar.

stablecoin issuer.definition: The company or organization that creates a stablecoin and manages the reserves backing its value.

stake.definition: The amount of a financial asset locked into a cryptocurrency protocol. It represents someone’s financial commitment to the protocol, their “skin in the game”.

staked.definition: The temporary commitment of a portion of your crypto into a smart contract for a specified amount of time in exchange for earning interest ("rewards").

staker.definition: A member of the Ethereum community, providing Ether to a validator node, in exchange for rewards.

stakers.definition: Members of the Ethereum community, providing Ether to validator nodes, in exchange for rewards.

staking.definition: The temporary commitment of a portion of your crypto into a smart contract for a specified amount of time in exchange for earning interest ("rewards").

staking pool.definition: On Ethereum: Smart contracts through which stakers provide Ether to another staker’s validator node.

staking providers.definition: Digital platforms providing staking services, usually through staking pools.

standard record.definition: A common data entry linked to an ENS domain, such as a wallet address, avatar, or email.

swap.definition: A trade from one token to another.

token.definition: Units that can stand for assets or deeds that are built on an existing blockchain.

token allowance.definition: An agreement between a wallet and smart contract, allowing limited or unlimited access to a specific token.

token approval.definition: Permission you grant a smart contract to move a specific token from your wallet; also called a token allowance.

token distribution.definition: The way in which tokens are allocated across different stakeholder groups.

token pair.definition: The two associated cryptocurrencies that make up a liquidity pool.

token swap.definition: A trade from one token to another.

tps.definition: (Transactions Per Second) A measure of a blockchain’s scalability: the number of transactions it processes per second.

trade.definition: Exchanging assets or money for something valuable; money verb on the skill cube.

trade route.definition: The path taken from starting token to ending token in a trade.

trade routing.definition: Planning the path taken from starting token to ending token in a trade.

transaction.definition: A record of transfer, monetary or otherwise, on the blockchain.

transaction finality.definition: The time it takes to be sure that a transaction is valid and final, meaning it won't be reversed or changed.

transaction hash.definition: The unique identifier for each transaction; it is derived from the transaction data, the digital signature of the transaction sender, and a one-time use number to avoid duplicate transactions.

transaction throughput.definition: How many transactions a blockchain can process at once, usually measured in transactions per second (TPS).

trustless.definition: The quality of operating without need to trust in people or institutions. (Automatic, not owned by any one person).

tvl.definition: (Total Value Locked) The overall amount of asset value stored in a specific place.

two factor authentication.definition: An extra layer of security used to make sure that people trying to gain access to an online account are who they say they are.

validating bridge.definition: A bridge contract that verifies withdrawals itself, removing the need to trust any external authority.

validator.definition: A participant in a Proof-of-Stake network who locks up stake to check transactions and propose blocks, earning rewards for honest work.

validator client.definition: The software a validator node runs to propose and check new blocks on a Proof-of-Stake network.

validator node.definition: A computer device run by a member of the Ethereum community. It processes transactions on the network in exchange for rewards.

validator nodes.definition: Computer devices run by members of the Ethereum community. They process transactions on the network in exchange for rewards.

validity proof.definition: A mathematical proof that a batch of transactions is correct, letting a blockchain verify it without redoing the work.

value-creation.definition: A business practice focused on generating innovative, high-quality products and services for users and the economy.

value-extraction.definition: A business practice where users are exploited through high fees, data harvesting, and unfair terms.

value-extractive.definition: A business practice where users are exploited through high fees, data harvesting, and unfair terms.

vault.definition: A smart contract that holds deposited tokens and puts them to work, giving depositors a token representing their share.

veto.definition: A vote in rejection of a governance proposal.

wallet.definition: A wallet is an application or device used to send and receive crypto assets on the blockchain.

wallet app.definition: An app on your computer or phone, used to connect to your wallet on the blockchain.

wallet provider.definition: The creator of the software you use to access your wallet. These providers do not own your wallet, but instead act as a bridge that lets you access your account on the blockchain.

web2.definition: The internet of centralized platforms and accounts, without blockchain infrastructure.

web3.definition: Refers to the internet of blockchains, where users can self-custody their assets & data.

yield farm.definition: A DeFi protocol where users deposit tokens to earn rewards. Yield farming means chasing the best of these rewards.

yourname.eth.definition: An example ENS name: a human-readable web3 username that points to your wallet address.

zero-knowledge.definition: Mathematical method that allows one party to prove a statement is valid without revealing any additional information about it.

zk rollup.definition: A Layer 2 rollup that uses zero-knowledge proofs to mathematically prove its batched transactions are valid on the Layer 1 blockchain.
